title: Rosh Hashanah: the books (Rosh Hashanah 16b)
hookLine: the Talmud pictures three books opened on the new year

cards: Leaving synagogue on Rosh Hashanah, people don't just say happy new year. They say: l'shanah tovah tikatevu, may you be written for a good year. Cards say it.
Text messages say it. After Rosh Hashanah the greeting shifts: g'mar chatimah tovah, may you be sealed for good. Written.
Sealed. It sounds like paperwork, and in a way it is. It comes from a single image in the Talmud: books lying open in heaven.

teach.b: In Rosh Hashanah 16b, Rabbi Kruspedai says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah.

teach.h: THE RIGHTEOUS, THE WICKED, THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: One for the completely righteous, one for the completely wicked, and one for those in between, the beinonim. The completely righteous are written and sealed at once, for life.
The completely wicked are written and sealed at once, for death.
Those in between are held, suspended, from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur: if they earn merit, they're written for life; if not, for death.
Now be honest: how many people do you know who are completely righteous, or completely wicked? Almost everyone is in the middle book. That's the point of the image.
The middle book is the open one, still being written, and the ten days ahead are for what goes in it. Maimonides, centuries later, turned this into advice.
A person should see themselves all year as exactly half good and half not, he said, and the whole world the same way.

teach.h: ONE ACT CAN TIP THE SCALE.
teach.b: Then any single good act could tip you, and the world, toward life.
The prayers of these days come back to the image again and again: remember us for life, and write us in the book of life. Then they give a reason: for Your sake, living God.
The request for life is made to the God of life. It's a frightening image, and it's meant to be. But it's also hopeful.

how: From Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, Jews add lines to the Amidah asking to be remembered and written in the book of life, and greet each other with 'l'shanah tovah tikatevu' and later 'g'mar chatimah tovah.'

o: the fast when the gates of heaven close
the new year, when the books of life are opened
the day a Torah scroll is finished and begun again

games.q: inside the three books — tap the pairs.
p: written and sealed for life at once
the in-between, held until Yom Kippur
may you be written for a good year
may you be sealed for good

s: the Talmud says everyone's fate is fixed on Rosh Hashanah
those in between are held open until Yom Kippur.
Maimonides advised seeing yourself as exactly half and half
so one good act could tip you, and the world, toward life.
the prayer to be written in the book of life gives a reason

games.q: you're one of the in-between, neither perfectly good nor truly wicked. Rosh Hashanah has come. where is your page?
games.why: the middle book stays open until Yom Kippur: the ten days are for what goes in it.

practice: Write one sentence you'd want in the book about you a year from now, on a scrap of paper or in your phone's notes: not a resolution about the gym, but something like she was kinder to her brother, or he finally called his father.
If you pray, you can ask to be written for a good year; if not, let the line be a direction.

wordCard.voice: Rosh Hashanah. The new year, when the Talmud says three books are opened, and most of us are in the middle one, still being written.

carryVoice: Your line: write us in. Written on Rosh Hashanah, sealed on Yom Kippur. That's day six hundred forty-nine.
